headline: AI regulation fears slam tech ETFs and VTS today while the Roosters clinch the NRL Grand Final in a thriller — markets mixed but long-term holdings remain solid.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS tracks the entire US share market in AUD, so it got hit from two sides today: US tech stocks fell last night on fears that the new Democrat-controlled Congress will push through tough AI regulation, and the Aussie dollar also dropped (making USD assets worth less in AUD terms when you convert back). The long-term case for US equities hasn't changed — this is short-term noise from a political shift.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: GXAI holds AI-focused companies and took a hit today as fears of incoming US AI regulation spooked the market. The concern is that new Democrat lawmakers plan to push a wave of AI regulation bills, which could slow growth for companies in this space. This ETF is already down 20% from what you paid for it — a painful position, but the structural AI growth story is still intact long term.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG is a diversified fund with heavy exposure to global (especially US) shares, so it dipped today alongside the broader global market sell-off driven by AI regulation fears. Nothing structurally wrong here — this is a normal reaction to global sentiment.

movers.name: DHHF.AX
movers.note: DHHF (a broad diversified ETF) eased back today in line with the ASX and global markets. No specific news catalyst — just general market softness flowing through. Long-term story unchanged.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE bucked the trend today, rising 1.19%. Emerging market stocks got a small lift partly because the weaker AUD makes their underlying assets worth more in local currency terms when translated back, and some investors rotated out of tech into broader global markets.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft slipped last night after two bits of tricky news: a data centre partner (IREN) disclosed it was delaying some AI deliveries to Microsoft, and reports emerged that Microsoft is winding down a deal to rent AI cloud capacity from Oracle. Neither is a business-breaker, but they add to the narrative that AI infrastructure spending may be getting harder to manage. Microsoft is still up nearly 20% on your total investment.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two edged up last night, buoyed by positive GTA 6 news flow — a former Rockstar tech director suggested the PC version could come sooner than expected to get ahead of AI-generated knockoffs, and Take-Two confirmed GTA Online will keep running when GTA 6 launches. Good signals for the game's commercial runway.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google had a solid night, rising 0.78% after a strong earnings recap highlighted three key takeaways: Google's ad business remains robust, its AI tools (Gemini) are driving engagement, and earnings beat expectations. A good result that reaffirms the long-term thesis.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara was flat today with no movement. The lithium market remains subdued — global lithium giant Albemarle's recent earnings call flagged it's focused on cost-cutting and waiting for demand to recover. No fresh catalyst for PLS either way today.

watch_today.title: AI regulation fears — biggest risk to your tech holdings this week
watch_today.detail: The incoming Democrat-controlled Congress is reportedly planning a flood of AI regulation bills. This spooked markets last night, hammering tech stocks and AI ETFs globally. Your GXAI.AX (already -20% from cost) and VTS.AX (tracks the whole US market) are most exposed. This is worth watching as the bills develop, but as a long-term holder, don't panic — regulation takes years to bite and the AI growth story is far from over.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX — hold despite the pain
watch_today.detail: GXAI dropped another 2.71% today and is now 20% underwater. The trigger is regulatory fear around AI, not a collapse in the underlying technology. For a long-term investor, this is uncomfortable but not a reason to sell. The AI sector will face volatility around regulation, but the structural tailwind remains. Sit tight unless you believe AI growth is fundamentally derailed.

watch_today.title: VTS.AX — solid long-term hold despite today's dip
watch_today.detail: VTS fell 2.67% today — a sharp single-session move driven by AI regulation fears hitting US tech stocks, plus a weaker AUD. But you're still slightly in the black overall (+1.4% total return). This fund holds the entire US market, so short-term policy noise doesn't change the long-term case. Hold comfortably.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX — lithium still in the doldrums
watch_today.detail: Pilbara was flat today but it's still down 58% from what you paid. Albemarle's Q3 earnings (the world's biggest lithium miner) flagged ongoing weak demand and a focus on cost discipline — not exactly a bullish backdrop. No fresh catalyst to buy more here. Hold and wait for the lithium cycle to turn, which most analysts expect as EV adoption picks up over the next few years.

watch_today.title: MSFT — minor wobble, long-term story intact
watch_today.detail: Microsoft dipped about 1% last night on some AI infrastructure headwinds (delayed data centre deliveries, an Oracle cloud deal unwinding). You're still up nearly 20% on your MSFT position. Nothing here changes the long-term investment case — Microsoft remains one of the best-placed AI plays globally. Hold.

watch_today.title: RBA rate hike — check your savings account
watch_today.detail: The RBA has hiked the cash rate again (November 2026), and savings account rates are being updated upward. If you have cash sitting in a low-rate account, now's a good time to shop around — some banks are passing the increase on faster than others.

world.summary: Big global stories today: Trump reshuffles his team after a midterm defeat, the Iran conflict continues to reshape energy and global trade, and US politics is set to fundamentally shift AI regulation.

stories.title: Trump names hardliner Stephen Miller as new Chief of Staff after midterm defeat
stories.why_it_matters: Donald Trump has replaced his Chief of Staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller following the Republicans' loss of control of Congress in the midterm elections. Miller is one of Trump's most hardline advisers, best known for architecting strict immigration policies during Trump's first term. The move signals Trump is doubling down on a confrontational political approach rather than moderating after the midterm defeat. For global markets and US allies like Australia, a more aggressive Trump political operation heading into 2028 could mean continued policy unpredictability.

stories.title: Iran war: Qatar mediating between US and Iran as conflict reshapes global energy
stories.why_it_matters: The 2026 Iran war is continuing to dominate global attention, with Qatar acting as a go-between in US-Iran mediation talks. The conflict is significantly disrupting global energy markets — oil near the Strait of Hormuz (a critical shipping lane for about 20% of the world's oil) remains under threat. Axios reports the war is also accelerating the renewables transition as countries scramble to reduce dependence on Middle Eastern oil. Oil is currently sitting at US$90.83 a barrel, up slightly, as supply concerns persist.

stories.title: Democrats plan wave of AI regulation bills after taking Congress
stories.why_it_matters: Following the US midterms, the incoming Democrat-controlled Congress is planning a sweeping package of AI regulation legislation. The prospect of new rules — which could include restrictions on how AI companies train models, use data, or deploy systems — triggered a multi-trillion dollar tech market sell-off this week, wiping billions from companies like Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta and Alphabet. For everyday investors with tech exposure, this is the biggest near-term political risk to watch. That said, regulation typically takes years to pass and implement in the US.

stories.title: US prosecutor who led Trump-backed election probe exits Justice Department
stories.why_it_matters: The special prosecutor who had been running a Trump-backed investigation into the 2024 US election has quietly left the Justice Department. The exit adds to growing controversy about the politicisation of federal law enforcement under Trump, with separate claims emerging that the Biden administration targeted Trump during the 2024 election. These ongoing legal and political battles are keeping the US political environment volatile heading into the next election cycle — which affects sentiment around US markets and policy stability.

markets.summary: The ASX slipped 0.49% today, dragged by global AI regulation fears. Last night on Wall Street, the NASDAQ actually climbed 1.09% and the S&P 500 edged up 0.31%, but that was despite significant losses in some AI-heavy stocks — tech gains were mixed. Gold pulled back nearly 1% and the Aussie dollar weakened, which hurts the value of AUD-denominated assets linked to US holdings.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Fell today, dragged by tech and growth stocks amid AI regulation fears flowing from the US.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Edged up last night — a modest gain despite significant volatility in AI-related stocks.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Rose last night — big tech names like Google helped lift the index even as AI regulation fears rattled some stocks.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Holding near $91 — the Iran conflict keeps upward pressure on oil prices.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold pulled back last night after a strong run — still at historically elevated levels above $4,000/oz.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar weakened — this makes your US holdings (GOOG, MSFT, TTWO) worth slightly less in AUD terms when you convert back.

politics.summary: Australian political commentary is dominated by what the US midterm results mean for Albanese, plus an RBA rate hike flowing through to savings accounts, a controversy over Senator Payman, and concerns about the AUKUS bill.

stories.title: US midterm result should 'scare' Albanese, say experts
stories.why_it_matters: Political analysts are warning Anthony Albanese to take note of the US midterms, where the Republicans lost control of Congress largely on cost-of-living anger. The Guardian reports Australia faces the same issues — housing affordability, inflation, and trust in government are all at troubling levels. With an Australian federal election due, the parallel is stark: voters who feel squeezed tend to punish incumbents.

stories.title: RBA hikes rates again — savings account rates moving up
stories.why_it_matters: The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) has lifted its cash rate again in November 2026, and banks are now adjusting savings account rates upward. If you have cash in a savings account, this is good news — but it's worth checking your bank is actually passing the increase on. For mortgage holders, though, another rate rise means higher repayments again.

stories.title: Senator Payman claims Albanese offered extra staff in exchange for her Senate vote
stories.why_it_matters: Independent Senator Fatima Payman has alleged that PM Anthony Albanese personally offered her extra parliamentary staff resources in exchange for her Senate vote. Payman — who left the Labor Party last year over the Gaza conflict — says the approach was inappropriate. The government denies any wrongdoing, but the allegation adds to pressure on Albanese at an already difficult political moment.

stories.title: AUKUS Bill hands sweeping powers to Defence Minister
stories.why_it_matters: New legislation tied to Australia's AUKUS submarine deal is coming under scrutiny for the sweeping powers it hands to the Defence Minister, bypassing normal oversight. Critics argue the bill gives one minister too much unchecked authority over multi-billion dollar decisions with limited parliamentary accountability. AUKUS is a cornerstone of Australia's defence strategy, but how the money and decisions are managed is increasingly under the microscope.

stories.title: Power bill blowout: taxpayers paid $5.5 billion in energy rebates
stories.why_it_matters: Sky News reports that Australian taxpayers have spent a staggering $5.5 billion on household energy rebates — well above initial projections. While the rebates were designed to soften the blow of surging electricity bills, the blowout raises questions about the long-term cost and whether the policy is sustainable. With inflation still a concern, this kind of fiscal pressure matters for the broader economy.

ai.summary: The biggest AI story this week is political: Democrats winning the US Congress has triggered a major AI regulation scare, hammering tech stocks. Meanwhile, OpenAI has launched a new model, GPT-6 Cyber.

stories.title: AI sell-off: Democrat Congress plans flood of AI regulation bills
stories.why_it_matters: The incoming Democrat majority in the US Congress is reportedly planning a large package of AI regulation bills, covering everything from how AI models are trained to how they're deployed. The mere prospect of regulation triggered a multi-trillion dollar sell-off in global tech stocks, wiping billions from companies like Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta and Alphabet. This is a major story for anyone with tech or AI holdings — though the actual laws will take years to pass and implement, and many may never get through the Senate.

stories.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Cyber — and it found security flaws hackers could exploit
stories.why_it_matters: OpenAI has released GPT-6 Cyber, a new specialised AI model positioned to compete with Anthropic's Claude Mythos and Google's Gemini. What makes this version notable is that it's specifically designed for cybersecurity use — and in testing, it was able to identify real security flaws that hackers could potentially exploit. That's a double-edged sword: useful for defence teams, but also a warning that AI is becoming a more powerful tool for both sides of the cybersecurity battle.

stories.title: Political shift reshapes the future of AI regulation globally
stories.why_it_matters: Beyond the immediate market reaction, analysts are examining how the US political shift — from Republican to Democrat control of Congress — could reshape AI policy not just in the US but globally. Under Republicans, AI regulation was largely hands-off. Democrats tend to favour more oversight, consumer protections, and accountability rules. If strong US AI laws pass, they tend to set a global benchmark, influencing how Australia and others approach their own AI policy.

sport.summary: The Roosters have won the 2026 NRL Grand Final in a one-point thriller over the Knights, Kyrgios is confirmed for 2027, and there's big NRL player news around Addo-Carr and Nathan Cleary.

stories.title: Roosters win 2026 NRL Grand Final 19-18 over the Knights
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters have claimed the 2026 NRL premiership, defeating the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in a Grand Final classic at Accor Stadium last Sunday. It was a one-point margin at fulltime — as close as it gets. Fox Sports reporter ringside described it as a haunting spectacle, with the Koloamatangi vs Leniu rivalry adding serious spice to proceedings. A memorable night for Roosters fans.

stories.title: Eels make huge call on Josh Addo-Carr's future after drugs test twist
stories.why_it_matters: The Parramatta Eels have made a major call on winger Josh Addo-Carr's future following a drugs test controversy. The article does not detail the specific outcome but describes it as a 'huge call' — suggesting either a contract termination or a significant extension with conditions attached. Addo-Carr's situation has been one of the biggest off-season stories in the NRL.

stories.title: Nathan Cleary facing another operation — and rejects huge offer
stories.why_it_matters: Panthers and Blues halfback Nathan Cleary is set for another surgery, raising fresh concerns about his long-term durability. News.com.au also reports Cleary has rejected an 'astonishing' financial offer — believed to be linked to either a US NFL inquiry or a rival NRL club — with reports suggesting he won't be leaving Penrith. His health and availability will be a major story heading into the 2027 season.

stories.title: Nick Kyrgios confirms he'll play on in 2027 despite difficult season
stories.why_it_matters: Nick Kyrgios has dispelled retirement rumours by confirming he will play in his first tournament of 2027. It's been a difficult 2026 season for the Canberran — dealing with suspension and what appeared to be a Wimbledon farewell. His first 2027 event has been confirmed, though the specific tournament isn't yet named. Good news for Australian tennis fans who've been wondering if he's finally hanging up the racket.
